pages.heading: Young Brazilians know they should invest. They just don't feel ready.
lines: My final thesis in Visual Design at UFRGS: a mobile app that makes learning about investing feel possible, practical and trustworthy for young first-time investors.
**Project:** Final thesis (TCC), UFRGS
**My role:** UX research, product design, prototyping
**Advisor:** Prof. Sandro Fetter
**Platform:** Mobile app (iOS & Android)

pages.heading: The problem: interest is up, confidence isn't
lines: Young Brazilians are joining the stock market, but financial literacy is still low, and most people don't invest at all.
Learning tools fall short: most stock market learning apps are rated below 3.9 stars, and brokers' tools sit behind paywalls. The challenges:
- little trust, and investing feels complicated
- jargon and technical content
- theory that never turns into practice

pages.heading: A full design cycle, start to finish
lines: The project went from discovery to a tested high-fidelity prototype, using Design Thinking with Lean Inception to scope an MVP.
I wanted to understand not just what people needed to learn, but how they take in financial information, and what stops them.

stops.name: Discover
stops.role: Market data, app benchmarks, expert consultation

pages.heading: Listening first
lines: I started from data: ANBIMA's “Raio X do Investidor 2022” survey on how Brazilians save and invest, plus B3 and Febraban studies.
I benchmarked three apps that teach or simulate investing, looking at visuals, structure and usability.
And I consulted two market experts, an investment advisor and an economist, about what each investor profile needs.

items.label: people in the ANBIMA survey I analyzed
apps benchmarked: TradeMap, Trading Game and Forex Game
market experts consulted: an advisor and an economist

pages.heading: What the research said
lines: Put together, the data, the benchmark and the experts pointed to four findings.
The biggest one: before talking about the stock market, the app had to teach financial education, because most people struggle to save in the first place.

items.title: Most people don't invest at all.
items.body: 69% don't save or invest, mostly for lack of money; lack of interest (8%) and insecurity (7%) come next.

items.title: Jargon is the wall.
items.body: Experts said stock market knowledge is low, and the hardest part is understanding the technical terms.

items.title: Safety comes first.
items.body: Security is the top reason for choosing a product, and most investors are conservative, afraid to lose what they have.

items.title: Learning tools fall short.
items.body: Learning apps are poorly rated, and the good tools from brokers are paid.

pages.heading: Two people to design for
lines: From the research came two personas: one driven by curiosity and learning, the other by practical goals and caution.
Empathy maps helped me see their emotional triggers and what might stop them, so the app could answer both.

items.name: Clara, the beginner
items.about: Young and ambitious, always looking to grow. Busy, but willing to put in the time to learn about money.
context: Little time to study: works full time
behavior: Looks for new, interactive ways to learn about investing
Open to digital tools that improve her money skills

items.name: Lucas, the cautious
items.about: Prefers proven methods, values security, and wants evidence before he decides anything.

pages.heading: Mapping the ups and downs
lines: I mapped both personas' journeys from curiosity to action: what they do, feel and ask at every stage.
The dips showed where support had to step in, so the app is built on progressive disclosure: one small step at a time, with help at the hard parts.

stages.name: Discovery
stages.doing: Finds the app, gets excited by interactive learning, goes through onboarding and signs up.
stages.feeling: Excited that it could help her build real money skills.

stages.name: Learning
stages.doing: Explores the learning tracks in her free time and picks up the basics.
stages.feeling: Some concepts are hard, but the app's resources help her through.

stages.name: Applying
stages.doing: Uses the simulator to try scenarios, then makes better decisions about her own money.
stages.feeling: Gains confidence, and that keeps her learning.

stages.name: Keeping up
stages.doing: Follows market news, manages her profile and takes the investor profile test.
stages.feeling: Market swings are unsettling, but up-to-date news helps her adapt.

stages.name: Discovery
stages.doing: Finds the app, drawn by its promise of reliable information and proven ways to protect his money, and signs up.
stages.feeling: Some resistance to a new approach, eased by trustworthy, evidence-based information.

stages.name: Learning
stages.doing: Works through tracks on protecting his money: diversification, emergency funds, saving.
stages.feeling: Feels secure in his decisions, and values how easy the app is to use.

stages.name: Applying
stages.doing: Uses the simulator to weigh scenarios and risks, and follows the market news.
stages.feeling: Market swings are hard, but up-to-date news helps him decide and adapt.

stages.name: Keeping up
stages.doing: Applies what he learned to his own finances and uses his profile for guidance that fits his investor type.
stages.feeling: Confident he's making safe decisions, without unnecessary risks.

pages.heading: Learn, practice, explore
lines: The app is organized around three pillars, so learning always leads to doing:
- **Learn:** learning tracks, from financial education to the stock market
- **Practice:** quizzes, exercises and an investment simulator
- **Explore:** market news and indicators, for context

variants.label: Learn
variants.note: Home shows where you left off and your progress; each track is a series of short lessons.

variants.label: Practice
variants.note: A quiz closes each lesson, and a simulator lets you try investing without risking real money.

variants.label: Explore
variants.note: Market news and indices for context, and short articles that explain the ideas behind each lesson.

pages.heading: Learning by doing
lines: Every lesson ends with a quiz and a practical exercise, so theory turns into something people can use.
Feedback is always encouraging, in plain language, and the right answer comes with a short explanation.
Try one of the app's real questions:

poll.title: Quiz time
poll.question: What is the 50-30-20 method?

options.label: A way to split your income in three

poll.reveal: It splits your net income: 50% for essentials, 30% for personal spending and 20% for savings and goals. It's one of the first lessons in the Financial Education track.
poll.prompt: Pick one to see the answer.

pages.heading: Friendly on purpose
lines: The brand had to lower the intimidation around investing. “Bora” is Brazilian slang for “let's go”: an invitation to act, in an everyday tone.
Neutrals and soft greens suggest growth and trust, Work Sans keeps things clear and friendly, and all the copy uses short sentences and encouraging verbs.
Everything lives in a Figma style guide, built for consistency and accessibility.

font.name: Work Sans
font.note: Regular to Bold, from display to text sizes

pages.heading: Testing with 10 people
lines: I tested the prototype in Maze with 10 people aged 18 to 35 with little investing knowledge, across four tasks: sign in, finish a lesson's quiz, simulate an investment, and find the IBOVESPA index.
I scored each task with the Single Usability Metric (SUM), which combines completion, time, errors and satisfaction. Every task scored above 96%, and Maze rated the test's usability 88.
Two changes came out of it: onboarding that advances with a tap, like Stories, and market indices right on the Home.
